items.value: Gains from economic reforms reach agriculture more slowly than they reach the other sectors of the economy
items.reasoning: The passage's whole structure is a contrast across the same decades: non-agricultural growth 'consistently increased from the 1980s to 2000s' while agriculture, after its 1980s spurt, stagnated. The corollary of one sector rising through the reform decades while the other flattens is that the benefit reaches agriculture far more slowly. B is not supportable because the passage never mentions the green revolution and in fact places the best decade in the 1980s, after it. C fails because no other country is compared anywhere in the passage. D asserts a cause (migration) the passage never raises.

The passage reports growth rates only; it offers no diagnosis of why agriculture stagnated and proposes no remedy, so no assumption about what would have closed the gap can be drawn from it. Assumption I imports a specific policy prescription (commercial crops, corporate farming) that the text never touches. Assumption II is stronger still - free insurance for all crops and subsidies 'at par with developed countries' - and is nowhere implied. Hence neither is valid.

items.value: The handloom industry must be freed from the narrow framing that ties it only to preserving cultural heritage
items.reasoning: The author's chain is explicit: handloom is equated with tradition, that single linear notion of tradition is now strongly contested, and 'when we promote handloom as a traditional industry, it is not surprising that large sections of our population choose to ignore it.' The remedy that follows is to stop confining handloom to the heritage narrative. B is the position the passage is arguing against. C (modernised organised industry) and D (machine-made products) propose changes to the product or the unit that the passage never discusses - its subject is the narrative, not the loom.

Assumption I overstates the passage: it says the tradition idea 'provides a legitimate basis for the State to support the sector' and criticises the framing, not State involvement itself, so it never implies the State should withdraw entirely. Assumption II misreads the cause: people ignore handloom because of how it is promoted (as a traditional industry tied to a contested narrative), not because the products have lost their appeal. Neither follows.

Multiples of 9 are already multiples of 3, so the condition reduces to 'not divisible by 2, 3, 5 or 7'. By inclusion-exclusion among 1 to 100: 50+33+20+14 = 117, minus the pairs (16+10+7+6+4+2 = 45) gives 72, plus the triples (3+2+1 = 6) gives 78 divisible by at least one. So 100 - 78 = 22. Listing confirms it: 1 together with the 21 primes from 11 to 97.

items.value: None of the above - the correct ratio is -5, which is not among the printed options
items.reasoning: The maximum of (x + y) is 8 + 7 = 15. The minimum of (x - y) takes the smallest x with the largest y, i.e. 4 - 7 = -3. The ratio is 15 / (-3) = -5, which appears nowhere in the list, so 'None of the above' is correct. Option B (15/2) comes from wrongly using the smallest positive difference 4 - 2 = 2, and option C (-15/2) from using -2; both ignore that y may be as large as 7 while x is as small as 4.

items.value: 5 possible values of k, namely 2, 3, 7, 13 and 19
items.reasoning: Only p = 2 and p = 3 are usable, since 5 squared is already 25 and 25 + k cannot stay prime below 30 for any prime k. With p = 2 the sum 4 + k is prime and under 30 for k = 3 (7), 7 (11), 13 (17) and 19 (23). With p = 3 the sum 9 + k is prime and under 30 only for k = 2 (11). Collecting the distinct k values gives {2, 3, 7, 13, 19}, that is 5.

items.value: More than 8 such sets exist (32 sets of three distinct integers)
items.reasoning: 1001 = 7 x 11 x 13, so every member must be one of its 8 divisors. LCM 1001 requires each prime to appear in at least one member and HCF 1 requires each prime to be missing from at least one, so for each of the three primes the pattern of presence across the three numbers is any of the 2^3 - 2 = 6 non-constant patterns, giving 6^3 = 216 ordered triples. Removing the 24 ordered triples with a repeated member leaves 192, i.e. 192/6 = 32 sets of three distinct integers (40 if repeats are allowed). Either way the count far exceeds 8, so 'More than 8' is the answer; examples include {1, 7, 143}, {1, 11, 91}, {7, 11, 13} and {77, 91, 143}.

Writing the subtraction out, (100P + 10Q + R) - (10P + S) = 110P + T reduces with Q = 3 to R - S - T = 20P - 30. Since R - S - T can never reach 10, P must be 1, giving S + T = R + 10. With T < 6 and all of P = 1, Q = 3, R, S, T distinct and non-zero, T can only be 2, 4 or 5; T = 2 forces S = R + 8 which is impossible, T = 4 gives (R, S) = (2, 8) and T = 5 gives (2, 7) and (4, 9). The three cases check out as 132 - 18 = 114, 132 - 17 = 115 and 134 - 19 = 115.

The 18-character string is the block ABBCCC repeated three times: ABBCCC ABBCCC ABBCCC. Overlaying that on AB_CC_A_BCCC_BBC_C, every printed letter agrees, and the five gaps at positions 3, 6, 8, 13 and 17 must be B, C, B, A and C respectively. Option A fails at the fourth gap, which begins the third block and must be A, not C.

items.value: The classroom must be reimagined and teaching re-invented
items.reasoning: The passage closes on exactly this - 'Higher learning is all about how to think rather than what to think. Teaching has to be re-invented' - after listing the new capacities (critical thinking, learning by doing, evidence-based argument) that exam-oriented teaching does not build. C overstates it: the passage asks for the classroom to change, not to be abolished. B lifts one quoted clause about government policy and inflates it into a demand for autonomy from government control. A raises resources, which the passage never mentions.

items.value: Only assumption I is valid - higher education must keep evolving in step with new developments in society
items.reasoning: The passage's argument rests on assumption I: it is precisely because 'the new demands of society and the future of work' call for different capacities that teaching must be re-invented, so higher education is taken to be something that has to move with society. Assumption II is not valid because funding is never mentioned anywhere in the passage. The judgement call is I's phrase 'all spheres of society', which is broader than the passage's 'society and the future of work', but the direction is the passage's own and no other option is defensible.

items.value: Converting plant food into animal food is a highly inefficient way of feeding people compared with eating grain and plant food directly
items.reasoning: The passage states the point outright and then quantifies it: grains and legumes that could feed humans directly are diverted into animal feed, and 'this conversion of plant-based food into animal food for humans is far from efficient' - only 16% of calories recovered from chickens, and 5 to 7% from large animals. A and C convert that observation into policy demands (a public policy on cereals, replacing animal protein) that the passage never makes. D declares inequality inevitable, whereas the passage treats it as a problem, not a given.

items.value: Only assumption II is valid - wealthier societies lose a great deal of food calories by routing their produce through animals
items.reasoning: Assumption II is simply the passage restated: as societies grow wealthier they eat more animal products, and that indirect route recovers only 16% of the calories from chickens and 5 to 7% from large animals, which is a large calorie loss. Assumption I is about what food manufacturing and processing industries in every country ought to do - a prescription for a different set of actors that the passage never introduces, since its subject is the conversion of crops into animal feed, not processing industries.

35^n needs n fives and n sevens. Counting sevens: 7 gives 1, 343 gives 3, 385 = 5 x 7 x 11 gives 1, 2401 gives 4 and 77777 = 7 x 41 x 271 gives 1, a total of 10. Counting fives: only 385 (one 5) and 1000 = 2^3 x 5^3 (three 5s), a total of 4. The limiting prime is 5, so the maximum n is 4.

The successive multipliers form the arithmetic run 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5. Taking X = 12: 24 x 0.5 = 12, 12 x 1 = 12, 12 x 1.5 = 18, 18 x 2 = 36 and 36 x 2.5 = 90, which reproduces every printed term. No other option makes the later ratios (18 to 36 to 90, i.e. 2 and 2.5) fall into a regular progression.

Walking in opposite directions their relative speed is 5 + 3 = 8 rounds per hour, so they meet once every 1/8 hour, i.e. every 7.5 minutes from 5:00 a.m. The meetings therefore fall at 7.5, 15, 22.5, 30 ... minutes past 5:00. Strictly between 5:20 a.m. (20 min) and 7:00 a.m. (120 min) the meeting times are 22.5 through 112.5, which is 13 crossings; equivalently, 100 minutes at 8 crossings per hour gives 13.33, so 13 complete crossings. Note the boundary: they do meet again exactly at 7:00 a.m. back at the start, so a reading that counts 7:00 itself would give 14 - I have answered the word 'between' as excluding the endpoint.

Substituting each option and applying the usual order of operations: A (SPRQ) gives 60/15 + 3x20 - 4 = 4 + 60 - 4 = 60; B (QRPS) gives 60 - 15x3 + 20/4 = 60 - 45 + 5 = 20; C (QRSP) gives 60 - 45/20 + 4 = 61.75; D (SPQR) gives 4 + 3 - 80 = -73. Only B equals 20.

Overtaking means the tram covers its own length at the relative speed. With tram speed v km/hr, the length is (v - 3) x 5/18 x 8 and also (v - 4) x 5/18 x 9, so 8(v - 3) = 9(v - 4), giving v = 12 km/hr. Substituting back, the length is 9 x 5/18 x 8 = 20 m, and the check against Y agrees: 8 x 5/18 x 9 = 20 m.

The palindromic pattern 1, 121, 12321, 1234321 ... comes from squaring repunits, and 12345678987654321 is the one that peaks at 9, so N = 111111111, a repunit of nine 1s. Direct multiplication confirms 111111111 squared = 12345678987654321. A digit-count check agrees: the square has 17 digits, so N must have 9.
